claim: Lung cancer had more than 2.2 million new cases diagnosed worldwide in 2020.
source: In this paper, we focus on modeling tumor-stroma interactions in lung cancer which is one of the most common and deadly cancers, with more than 2.2 million new cases diagnosed and 1.8 million deaths worldwide in 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement about epidemiological data that is presented as established information in the manuscript.

claim: Lung cancer had 1.8 million deaths worldwide in 2020.
source: In this paper, we focus on modeling tumor-stroma interactions in lung cancer which is one of the most common and deadly cancers, with more than 2.2 million new cases diagnosed and 1.8 million deaths worldwide in 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement about epidemiological data that is presented as established information in the manuscript.

claim: Non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) accounts for 85% of lung cancers.
source: Non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) accounts for the vast majority of lung cancers (85%) (Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sung et al., 2021.

claim: The tumor-stroma ratio is an independent prognostic factor in cancer.
source: Indeed, the tumor-stroma ratio turns out to be an independent prognostic factor, with a large proportion of stroma leading to a worse prognosis (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2016.

claim: A large proportion of stroma leads to a worse prognosis in cancer.
source: Indeed, the tumor-stroma ratio turns out to be an independent prognostic factor, with a large proportion of stroma leading to a worse prognosis (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2016.

claim: Fibroblasts and macrophages are the majority of cells that make up the stroma.
source: The majority of cells that make up the stroma are fibroblasts and macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Fibroblasts and macrophages can act as both tumor promoters and tumor suppressors depending on the stage of tumor progression and mutational status.
source: Both types are affected and reprogrammed by cancer cells and have been shown to act as tumor promoters and tumor suppressors, depending on the stage of tumor progression and of its mutational status (Schreiber et al., 2011; Coussens and Werb, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schreiber et al., 2011 and Coussens and Werb, 2002.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts produce higher levels of extracellular matrix compared to normal fibroblasts.
source: As cancer progresses, tumor cells often transform surrounding healthy fibroblasts into cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) which, similarly to a wound healing context, produce higher levels of extracellular matrix (ECM) as well as growth factors and cytokines that affect the recruitment of immune or vascular cells and the growth of cancer cells (Mathieson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mathieson et al., 2022.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts produce growth factors and cytokines that affect the recruitment of immune or vascular cells and the growth of cancer cells.
source: As cancer progresses, tumor cells often transform surrounding healthy fibroblasts into cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) which, similarly to a wound healing context, produce higher levels of extracellular matrix (ECM) as well as growth factors and cytokines that affect the recruitment of immune or vascular cells and the growth of cancer cells (Mathieson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mathieson et al., 2022.

claim: Activated fibroblasts produce fibers that act as a mechanical barrier around the tumor, impeding the movement of immune cells.
source: Activated fibroblasts produce fibers that act as a mechanical barrier around the tumor, impeding the movement of immune cells and limiting the interaction between cytotoxic T-cells and cancer cells (Salmon et al., 2012; Yaegashi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Salmon et al., 2012 and Yaegashi et al., 2021.

claim: Activated fibroblasts limit the interaction between cytotoxic T-cells and cancer cells.
source: Activated fibroblasts produce fibers that act as a mechanical barrier around the tumor, impeding the movement of immune cells and limiting the interaction between cytotoxic T-cells and cancer cells (Salmon et al., 2012; Yaegashi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Salmon et al., 2012 and Yaegashi et al., 2021.

claim: CAFs may prevent the spread of cancer by creating a mechanical barrier around tumors.
source: However, by creating such a barrier around tumors, CAFs may also prevent the spread of cancer, as mechanical stress can reduce cell spreading and promote cell apoptosis (Cheng et al., 2009; Barbazan et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2009 and Barbazan et al., 2023.

claim: Mechanical stress can reduce cell spreading and promote cell apoptosis.
source: However, by creating such a barrier around tumors, CAFs may also prevent the spread of cancer, as mechanical stress can reduce cell spreading and promote cell apoptosis (Cheng et al., 2009; Barbazan et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2009 and Barbazan et al., 2023.

claim: Biochemical factors expressed by CAFs help to modify the phenotype of T-cells or inactivate their cytotoxic capacity.
source: In addition, biochemical factors expressed by CAFs also help to modify the phenotype of T-cells or inactivate their cytotoxic capacity (Nazareth et al., 2007; Lakins et al., 2018; Koppensteiner et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nazareth et al., 2007, Lakins et al., 2018, and Koppensteiner et al., 2022.

claim: CAFs have an ambiguous role as both tumor promoters and tumor suppressors.
source: Thus, CAFs have an ambiguous role as tumor promoters, inhibiting T-cell invasion into the nest, and as tumor suppressors, limiting the cancer growth and giving rise to an immune-excluded tumor (Figure 2B), which is less proliferative than a free-growing tumor (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discussion of CAF functions in the manuscript.

claim: In NSCLC, the recruitment of CD8+ T-cells is modulated by a specific tumor-associated antigen present on the surface of cancer cells.
source: In the context of non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC), the recruitment of CD8 + T-cells seems to be modulated by a specific tumor-associated antigen present on the surface of the cancer cells (Hiraoka et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hiraoka et al., 2006.

claim: Interleukin-6 (IL6) and Interleukin-8 (IL8) stimulate the infiltration of CD8+ T-cells.
source: In particular, in the family of inflammatory proteins, also called cytokines, Interlukin-6 (IL6) and (IL8) seem, among others to stimulate the infiltration of CD8+ (Liu et al., 2022; McKeown et al., 2004; Brenner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2022, McKeown et al., 2004, and Brenner et al., 2017.

claim: CD8+ T-cells that infiltrate the tumor differentiate from both circulating and tissue-resident precursors.
source: The origins of CD8+ T-cells that infiltrate the tumor are diverse, as they differentiate from both circulating and tissue-resident precursors (Gueguen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gueguen et al., 2021.

claim: Chemokines produced by dendritic cells or cancer cells play an important role in attracting T-cells via chemotaxis.
source: Chemical factors also play an important role in attracting T-cells via chemotaxis, such as the chemokines produced by dendritic cells or cancer cells (Brown et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2007.

claim: In LUSC, fibroblasts occupy 35% of the stroma with a tumor stroma ratio (TSR) of 1.29.
source: Here, in the case of LUSC, we found that fibroblasts (composed of 6% ADH1B, 37% FAP+ αSMA, 25% FAP+ αSMA+, 31% FAP+ αSMA+) occupy 35% of the stroma with a tumor stroma ratio (TSR) of 1.29.
evidence: This claim is based on data measured by the authors from patient samples.

claim: In LUAD, fibroblasts occupy 31% of the stroma with a TSR of 1.07.
source: In LUAD, these proportions were partly modified: fibroblasts (composed of 48% ADH1B, 18% FAP+ αSMA−, 7% FAP++ αSMA+, 26% FAP− αSMA+) occupy 31% of the stroma, with a TSR of 1.07.
evidence: This claim is based on data measured by the authors from patient samples.

claim: FAP+ αSMA+ fibroblasts are most responsible for T-cell exclusion.
source: The fibroblasts most responsible for T-cell exclusion are shown to be FAP+ αSMA+(Grout et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grout et al., 2022.

claim: When FAP+ αSMA+ fibroblasts line the tumor, T-cells are excluded from it.
source: In Figure 3, we compare two microenvironments. In the top one, FAP+ αSMA+ are lining the tumor (Figure 3a, c, d), and T-cells are excluded from it (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from Figure 3 showing immunohistochemistry staining patterns.

claim: When no FAP+ αSMA+ fibroblasts are observed, T-cells infiltrate the tumor.
source: On the contrary, in cases where no FAP+ αSMA+ are observed, fibroblasts are homogeneously distributed in the stroma (Figure 3g, e, h), and T-cells infiltrate the tumor (Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from Figure 3 showing immunohistochemistry staining patterns.

claim: Lung cancer cells have a diameter between 13–18 μm.
source: In fact, cell types can vary greatly in size. For example, lung cancer cells have a diameter between 13–18 μm (Hosokawa et al., 2013), fibroblasts ∼16 μm (Mitsui and Schneider, 1976), and T-cells between 5–10 μm (Tasnim et al., 2018), resulting in volumes and projected areas that can be 10 times smaller for T-cells compared to fibroblasts and cancer cells for the same densities.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hosokawa et al., 2013.

claim: Fibroblasts have a diameter of approximately 16 μm.
source: In fact, cell types can vary greatly in size. For example, lung cancer cells have a diameter between 13–18 μm (Hosokawa et al., 2013), fibroblasts ∼16 μm (Mitsui and Schneider, 1976), and T-cells between 5–10 μm (Tasnim et al., 2018), resulting in volumes and projected areas that can be 10 times smaller for T-cells compared to fibroblasts and cancer cells for the same densities.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mitsui and Schneider, 1976.

claim: T-cells have a diameter between 5–10 μm.
source: In fact, cell types can vary greatly in size. For example, lung cancer cells have a diameter between 13–18 μm (Hosokawa et al., 2013), fibroblasts ∼16 μm (Mitsui and Schneider, 1976), and T-cells between 5–10 μm (Tasnim et al., 2018), resulting in volumes and projected areas that can be 10 times smaller for T-cells compared to fibroblasts and cancer cells for the same densities.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tasnim et al., 2018.

claim: T-cells have volumes and projected areas that can be 10 times smaller than fibroblasts and cancer cells for the same densities.
source: In fact, cell types can vary greatly in size. For example, lung cancer cells have a diameter between 13–18 μm (Hosokawa et al., 2013), fibroblasts ∼16 μm (Mitsui and Schneider, 1976), and T-cells between 5–10 μm (Tasnim et al., 2018), resulting in volumes and projected areas that can be 10 times smaller for T-cells compared to fibroblasts and cancer cells for the same densities.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited cell diameter measurements.

claim: The dynamical system model identifies two mechanisms that control tumor growth: competition with other species for resources and space, and the efficiency of the T-cell response.
source: More precisely, we demonstrate that two mechanisms control tumor growth: the competition with other species for resources and space, and the efficiency of the T-cell response.
evidence: This is a conclusion derived from the analysis of the dynamical system model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The spatial distribution of T-cells inside the tumor is an indicator of patient survival.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that the spatial distribution of T-cells inside the tumor is an indicator of the patient survival (Carstens et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carstens et al., 2017.

claim: When fibroblasts are activated, they make the environment around the tumor nest fibrotic with a mass fraction reaching 20-30%.
source: When fibroblasts are activated, they make the environment around the tumor nest fibrotic (Figure 5B and C), with a mass fraction around the nest reaching 20-30%.
evidence: This claim is based on the results of the spatial model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Even when T-cells are efficient, the fibroblast barrier precludes T-cells from the tumor.
source: At the same time, even in a situation where T-cells are efficient, the barrier precludes T-cells from the tumor (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on the results of the spatial model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: When T-cells are introduced without transformation from NAFs to CAFs, the tumor dies as cancer cells are eliminated.
source: When T-cells are introduced without transformation from NAFs to CAFs (Figure 5I-red curve), the tumor dies as cancer cells are eliminated and the compact nest disappears (Figure 5E- red curve).
evidence: This claim is based on the results of the spatial model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The model reproduces that cancer-associated fibroblasts act as a barrier to tumor expansion.
source: We reproduce that cancer-associated fibroblasts act as a barrier to tumor expansion, but also reduce the efficiency of the immune response.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model reproduces that cancer-associated fibroblasts reduce the efficiency of the immune response.
source: We reproduce that cancer-associated fibroblasts act as a barrier to tumor expansion, but also reduce the efficiency of the immune response.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The final outcome depends on the parameter values for each patient and leads to either tumor invasion, persistence, or eradication.
source: Our conclusion is that the final outcome depends on the parameter values for each patient and leads to either tumor invasion, persistence, or eradication as a result of the interplay between cancer cell growth, T-cell cytotoxicity, and fibroblast activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The tumor outcome results from the interplay between cancer cell growth, T-cell cytotoxicity, and fibroblast activity.
source: Our conclusion is that the final outcome depends on the parameter values for each patient and leads to either tumor invasion, persistence, or eradication as a result of the interplay between cancer cell growth, T-cell cytotoxicity, and fibroblast activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fibroblasts are often considered to be a major component of the stroma but are only found in small proportions in scRNA-seq with 10X single-cell systems.
source: The fibroblast population in the stroma, which is very heterogeneous and not easy to identify, is the best example. In particular, although fibroblasts are often considered to be a major component of the stroma, they are only found in small proportions in scRNA-seq with 10 X single-cell systems, which may be rather surprising.
evidence: This is an observation about discrepancies in measurement methods discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The low detection of fibroblasts in scRNA-seq may be due to tissue digestion processes, incomplete stroma extraction, and lower efficiency of 10X single-cell systems for fibroblasts.
source: This situation is well known and may be due to tissue digestion processes, to the fact that part of the stroma is not extracted with the tumor nodule, and to a lower efficiency of 10 X single-cell systems for fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed discrepancies in measurement methods.

claim: The study analyzed data from 13 patients with lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) and 22 patients with lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD).
source: In this study, we analyzed data from 13 patients with lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) and 22 patients with lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), based on a recent publication by some of the present authors (Grout et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the patient cohort used in the study.

claim: The dynamical system model uses a pressure-like term to avoid excessive proliferation.
source: In a first step, we ignore any spatial organization and model the proliferation and activation phenomena alone, while introducing a pressure-like term to avoid excessive proliferation.
evidence: This describes a feature of the mathematical model developed in the manuscript.

claim: The spatial model is based on Onsager's variational principle.
source: In a second step, we enrich the model by considering the spatio-temporal evolution of tumor growth through a continuum approach for cell mixtures based on Onsager's variational principle.
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework used for the spatial model.

claim: Cancer cells transform fibroblasts into cancer-associated fibroblasts.
source: Its structure and functions are altered during malignancy: tumor cells transform fibroblasts into cancer-associated fibroblasts, which exhibit immunosuppressive activities on which growth and metastasis depend.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts exhibit immunosuppressive activities on which growth and metastasis depend.
source: Its structure and functions are altered during malignancy: tumor cells transform fibroblasts into cancer-associated fibroblasts, which exhibit immunosuppressive activities on which growth and metastasis depend.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts exclude immune cells from the tumor nest.
source: These include exclusion of immune cells from the tumor nest, cancer progression, and inhibition of T-cell-based immunotherapy.
evidence: This is stated as one of the immunosuppressive activities of CAFs in the abstract.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts inhibit T-cell-based immunotherapy.
source: These include exclusion of immune cells from the tumor nest, cancer progression, and inhibition of T-cell-based immunotherapy.
evidence: This is stated as one of the immunosuppressive activities of CAFs in the abstract.

claim: The model incorporates data on the density of different cell types in the stroma using immunohistochemistry techniques on tumor samples from lung cancer patients.
source: To understand these complex interactions, we measure the density of different cell types in the stroma using immunohistochemistry techniques on tumor samples from lung cancer patients.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to inform the model.

claim: The model is a minimal dynamical system that explores the variety of outcomes in tumor-stroma interactions.
source: We incorporate these data into a minimal dynamical system, explore the variety of outcomes, and finally establish a spatio-temporal model that explains the cell distribution.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the manuscript.

claim: The spatio-temporal model explains the cell distribution in the tumor microenvironment.
source: We incorporate these data into a minimal dynamical system, explore the variety of outcomes, and finally establish a spatio-temporal model that explains the cell distribution.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the manuscript.

claim: Finite element-based simulations demonstrate the ambiguous activity of CAFs in regulating cancer cell proliferation and invasion.
source: Finite element-based simulations in two-dimensional space demonstrate the ambiguous activity of CAFs in regulating cancer cell proliferation and invasion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: CAFs undergo poorly reversible activation in absence of an appropriate therapy.
source: CAFs are characterized by their increased mobility, proliferation, and ECM remodeling and, unlike wound-associated fibroblasts, they seem to undergo poorly reversible activation in absence of an appropriate therapy (Nakamura et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2009; Peng et al., 2013; Kalluri, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2004, Wang et al., 2009, Peng et al., 2013, and Kalluri, 2016.

claim: CAFs are characterized by increased mobility, proliferation, and ECM remodeling.
source: CAFs are characterized by their increased mobility, proliferation, and ECM remodeling and, unlike wound-associated fibroblasts, they seem to undergo poorly reversible activation in absence of an appropriate therapy (Nakamura et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2009; Peng et al., 2013; Kalluri, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2004, Wang et al., 2009, Peng et al., 2013, and Kalluri, 2016.

claim: The diversity of the fibroblast population results from phenotypic modifications and explains their diverse functions and localization in the stroma.
source: The diversity of this population, resulting from phenotypic modifications, explains their diverse functions and localization in the stroma, close or distant from the tumor nest (Barrett and Puré, 2020; Grout et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barrett and Puré, 2020 and Grout et al., 2022.

claim: The model considers four different cell types: cancer cells, T-cells, activated fibroblasts, and non-activated fibroblasts.
source: As in the previous section, we consider four different cell types namely cancer cells, T-cells, activated and non-activated fibroblasts, with different attraction properties.
evidence: This describes the components of the spatial model.

claim: The model does not consider transformation of NAFs into CAFs as a reversible process.
source: Furthermore, our model does not consider transformation of NAFs into CAFs as a reversible process.
evidence: This is an assumption made in the model development.

claim: The mass fraction of CAFs reflects the amount of matrix produced by the fibroblasts.
source: In fact, the mass fraction of CAFs is assumed to reflect the amount of matrix produced by the fibroblasts, resulting in a very high friction in the medium.
evidence: This is an assumption made in the model development.

claim: In the case of a free-growing tumor with NAFs and inactive T-cells, cancer cell growth is not hindered by any obstacles.
source: As shown in Figure 5E and H (blue curve), in the case of a free-growing tumor, i.e., in the presence of NAFs and inactive T-cells, cancer cell growth is not hindered by any obstacles, so this is the most severe situation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The presence of a stroma plays a role in cancer cell growth by exerting pressure.
source: However, the tumor provokes the formation of a stroma composed of the NAFs and inefficient T-cells. The presence of a stroma plays a role in the cancer cell growth described in Equation 1 and leads to a growth that would be less important than in a case without stroma or composed only of NAFs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and G).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: When T-cell activity is marginalized by the presence of CAFs, two tumor nests slowly coalesce to form a single solid tumor nest.
source: When T-cell activity is marginalized by the presence of CAFs, the two nests slowly coalesce to form a single solid tumor nest (see Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the immune-inflamed tumor, the activity of T-cells reduces the ability of two nests to coalesce.
source: As expected, in the immune-inflamed tumor, the activity of T-cells reduces the ability of the two nests to coalesce by also reducing their mass fraction, leading to very low values of cancer cells (see Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the absence of T-cell chemotaxis, tumor growth is unrestricted and the nests create a larger tumor.
source: On the contrary, in the absence of T-cell chemotaxis, the tumor growth is unrestricted and the nests create a larger tumor by also increasing their mass fraction (see Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 6.

claim: Coalescence of tumor nests leads to anisotropic shapes of the tumor.
source: In the latter cases, coalescence leads to anisotropic shapes of the tumor.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: Relaxation to a round tumor shape is slower for large tumors and even more for fibrotic tumors where friction significantly slows down this process.
source: Although relaxation in our model eventually leads to a round shape, this relaxation is slower for large tumors and even more for fibrotic tumors where friction significantly slows down this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The density of the extracellular matrix is not always sufficient to induce T-cell exclusion.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that the density of the extracellular matrix is not always sufficient to induce T-cell exclusion (Carstens et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carstens et al., 2017.

claim: Matrix orientation strongly influences metastasis and tumor growth by providing directional cues.
source: At the same time, matrix orientation strongly influences metastasis and tumor growth by providing directional cues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: There is a strong difference in tumor outcome between fibers normal to the tumor surface and fibers along the tumor, both at the level of immune response and cancer escape.
source: Thus, there is a strong difference in the outcome of a tumor with fibers normal to the tumor surface and one with fibers along the tumor, both at the level of immune response and cancer escape.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the discussion of fiber orientation effects.

claim: The flux of cancer cells is much higher in the case of normal orientation of the fibers than in the case of parallel orientation.
source: In Figure 7B and C we show the nematic order of the matrix and the flux field of the cancer cells in the case of orthonormal and normal orientation with respect to the tumor nest boundary, and due to the influx of fibroblasts from the right side of the system. The flux of cancer cells is much higher in the case of normal orientation of the fibers than in the case of parallel orientation.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 7.

claim: The model focuses on early tumor growth prior to angiogenesis.
source: In our article, the focus is on early tumor growth prior to angiogenesis and the development of its stroma rich in T-cells and fibroblasts, the activation of non-activated fibroblasts into cancer-associated fibroblasts and the marginalization of T-cells from the tumor nest.
evidence: This describes the scope of the model.

claim: The model does not consider the fibers of the extracellular matrix as a component per se, but considers them through the friction increase.
source: In this study, we did not consider the fibers of the extracellular matrix as a component per se, but we considered them through the friction increase.
evidence: This describes a modeling choice made in the manuscript.

claim: Identifying the different scenarios that can occur in the TME and their likelihood is critical to predict the outcome of therapy.
source: Identifying the different scenarios that can occur in the TME and their likelihood is critical to predict the outcome of therapy (Mori and Ben Amar, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mori and Ben Amar, 2023.

claim: Both pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics are highly dependent on the spatial structure and composition at the tumor site.
source: Indeed, both pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics are highly dependent on the spatial structure and composition at the tumor site.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Classification and quantitative characterization of the various outcomes can help to monitor the treatment in real-time according to the evolution of the TME.
source: Classification and quantitative characterization of the various outcomes can also help to monitor the treatment in real-time according to the evolution of the TME.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the modeling approach.
